reference.source: Manson's Tropical Diseases / Mandell, Douglas and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
clinicalPearls: Pinta is a chronic non-venereal treponematosis caused by Treponema carateum and is confined to the skin, occurring in remote rural areas of Central and South America
Transmission is by prolonged direct skin-to-skin contact with lesion material, favoured by crowding and poor hygiene; it is not sexually transmitted
Unlike the other endemic treponematoses, pinta affects only the skin and does not involve bone, viscera or the nervous system
The primary lesion is an erythematous scaly papule or plaque that slowly enlarges, usually on exposed limbs
Secondary lesions (pintids) are disseminated scaly patches that undergo striking colour changes, becoming blue, violet, brown then depigmented
Late pinta is characterised by symmetrical achromic (depigmented) and atrophic patches that resemble vitiligo and are cosmetically disfiguring
Diagnosis uses dark-field microscopy and treponemal/non-treponemal serology (indistinguishable from syphilis); treatment for the endemic treponematoses is benzathine penicillin
reference.pathophysiology: Treponema carateum enters through breaks in the skin during prolonged close contact. It multiplies locally to form the primary lesion and then, over months, produces disseminated secondary skin lesions (pintids) through local and lymphatic spread. The immune response and disturbance of melanocytes produce the characteristic sequence of dyschromic changes, progressing from hyperpigmentation to permanent depigmentation and skin atrophy in late disease. Because the organism does not disseminate to deep tissues, pinta remains a purely cutaneous disease throughout its course.
additionalDifferentials: Pityriasis versicolor and other superficial mycoses
Psoriasis or chronic eczema (for scaly plaques)
additionalInvestigations: Dark-field microscopy of scrapings from active lesions for spirochaetes
Non-treponemal serology (e.g. RPR/VDRL) for activity and follow-up
Skin biopsy where the diagnosis is uncertain
PCR of lesion material where available
Assessment of close contacts in endemic communities
redFlags: Extensive disfiguring depigmentation causing psychosocial harm
Diagnostic uncertainty with vitiligo or leprosy delaying treatment
Positive syphilis serology raising confusion about venereal infection
Persistence or spread of active lesions despite treatment
reference.prognosis: Early and secondary pinta respond fully to penicillin, but late achromic and atrophic skin changes are often permanent and cosmetically disfiguring even after cure; the disease carries no systemic morbidity.
pitfalls: Mistaking late depigmented lesions for vitiligo and missing a treatable infection
Interpreting positive treponemal serology as venereal syphilis
Expecting depigmented skin to re-pigment fully after treatment
Failing to treat contacts and interrupt transmission
Confusing pinta with other endemic treponematoses without regional context
references: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
